neighbors.heading: sweet is your will
neighbors.text: Today Rama lost a kingdom in one sentence and said, so be it, I'll go. Sikhs have a word for meeting what comes: hukam, the order of God's will running through everything. The Japji says all are within the hukam, and none outside it. Guru Arjan goes further and calls that will sweet. Accepting it, for a Sikh, is trust in the one who sends.
neighbors.difference: Rama bows to a promise his father made, a son keeping a king's human word. For Sikhs, the hukam is God's own will, and accepting it goes hand in hand with standing up for what's right.
neighbors.shared: you can lose something big and still keep your heart steady.
neighbors.sources: Japji Sahib, pauri 2, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 1 (paraphrase) · Guru Arjan, Raag Asa, Guru Granth Sahib (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: not my will
neighbors.text: Today Rama heard he must leave everything, and answered, so be it. Christians remember a night in a garden. Before his arrest, Jesus asked that the cup might pass from him, and then prayed: "nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done." The Gospel doesn't pretend it was easy. He asked first, and then he said yes.
neighbors.difference: Rama keeps his father's promise to Kaikeyi, a son honoring a king's word. Christians hear Jesus speaking to God as Father on the way to the cross, and believe his yes opened salvation to the world.
neighbors.shared: calm can be a choice made while it still hurts.

neighbors.heading: a prince who gave it all
neighbors.text: Today Rama gave his wealth away on the day his life fell apart, and still had a joke for a poor old man. Buddhists tell of a giving prince too. In the Vessantara Jataka, a story of one of the Buddha's past lives, Prince Vessantara gives so freely that he's sent into exile in the forest, and keeps giving there. Buddhists call giving dana.
neighbors.difference: Rama gives before exile so no one who depends on him is left without support, keeping a prince's dharma. Vessantara's giving is told as practice toward awakening, letting go even of what he loves most.
neighbors.shared: grief doesn't have to make your hands close.

neighbors.heading: a cheerful giver
neighbors.text: Today Rama made a poor man throw his staff, gave him every cow up to where it landed, then apologized for the joke. Catholics hear Saint Paul in that: "for God loveth a cheerful giver." The Church counts giving to the poor among the works of mercy, and saints like Francis of Assisi gave away everything they had.
neighbors.difference: Rama gives as a prince leaving home, caring for those who depend on him. For Catholics, a gift to someone in need is also a gift to Christ himself, who said what you do for the least, you do for him.
neighbors.shared: a gift lands best when the other person keeps their dignity.
neighbors.sources: 2 Corinthians 9:7 (Douay-Rheims) · Matthew 25:40 (paraphrase) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2447 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: another self
neighbors.text: Today Guha, a forest king, came out to meet Rama, and the text calls him a friend as dear as life. Philosophers have tried to name that kind of friend. Aristotle said the best friendship isn't for usefulness or fun, but for the other person's own good, and he called such a friend another self. Guha offers a kingdom and asks nothing back.
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, Rama is God, and later devotion counts friendship as one way of loving God. For Aristotle, friendship is a human good, part of a well-lived life, that needs nothing beyond itself.
neighbors.shared: the best friends want your good, not your use.

neighbors.heading: loved as his own soul
neighbors.text: Today Guha met Rama at the river, a friend as dear as life. The Hebrew Bible tells of a prince who loved like that. When Jonathan, son of King Saul, met David, "the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul." He gave David his own robe and his sword.
neighbors.difference: Guha offers Rama his kingdom, and Rama turns it down to keep his vow. Jonathan, heir to a throne, knows David will be king one day, and loves him anyway, even against his own father.
neighbors.shared: a true friend is glad to see you rise.

items.lessonTitle: Dasharatha's death and the curse that caused it (Shravana Kumara)

neighbors.heading: honor thy father and mother
neighbors.text: Today a boy with no name in the oldest text became Shravan Kumar, the son who cared for his blind parents. Christians carry a commandment for that love. Paul repeats it to the church at Ephesus: "Honour thy father and mother; which is the first commandment with promise." Elsewhere he asks believers to care for their own families, repaying their parents.
neighbors.difference: Shravan's story grew in later retellings into a byword for a devoted son. For Christians, honoring parents is one of the Ten Commandments given by God, and Jesus also asks that love for him come first.
neighbors.shared: the hands that once carried us deserve to be carried.

neighbors.heading: the wing of mercy
neighbors.text: Today we met the boy later tellings call Shravan Kumar, who carried water to his blind parents. The Qur'an speaks to that same care. When parents grow old, it says, don't speak harshly to them: "lower unto them the wing of submission through mercy," and pray, "My Lord! Have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little."
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, Shravan's devotion is a picture of a son's dharma. In the Qur'an, kindness to parents comes right after the command to worship God alone, so caring for them is part of worship itself.
neighbors.shared: parents growing old is a call to grow gentle.

neighbors.heading: servant of the servants
neighbors.text: Today Bharata ruled for fourteen years and refused to be king, laying every decision before his brother's sandals. Catholics know that shape. Jesus taught that whoever wants to be first must be the servant of the rest. Popes still use an old title, servant of the servants of God, and the Church speaks of keeping watch until Christ comes again.
neighbors.difference: Bharata keeps a throne for a brother who will walk back through the gate. Catholics believe Christ is present now, in the sacraments and the Church, even as they wait for his return.
neighbors.shared: the one in charge can be the one who serves.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 20:26–27 (paraphrase) · servus servorum Dei, a papal title (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the Guru on the throne
neighbors.text: Today a pair of sandals sat on Ayodhya's throne, and Bharata held the royal umbrella over them himself. In a gurdwara, Sikhs see something like it. The Guru Granth Sahib rests on a raised throne under a canopy, and someone waves a whisk, a chaur, above it, as for a sovereign. Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh named the scripture the Guru.
neighbors.difference: The sandals stand in for Rama until he comes home. For Sikhs, the Guru Granth Sahib stands in for no one: it is the living Guru, the word itself, and Sikhs bow to it as such.
neighbors.shared: honoring someone absent can keep them present.

neighbors.heading: no talebearing
neighbors.text: Today Rama stopped his brother mid-sentence: don't speak badly of our middle mother; speak of Bharata. Judaism has a whole teaching about that. The Torah says, "Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people." The rabbis call harmful talk lashon hara, the evil tongue, and warn against it even when it's true.
neighbors.difference: Rama refuses bitterness out of love for a family that wronged him, a son's dharma. Jewish law works it out in detail: what may and may not be said, and when speaking up is needed to protect someone.
neighbors.shared: some words protect a family by never being said.

neighbors.heading: right speech
neighbors.text: Today Lakshmana said one sentence too many about Kaikeyi, and Rama turned the talk back to Bharata. Buddhists count speech as part of the path itself. Right speech, the Buddha taught, means no lying, no talk that divides people, no harsh words, and no idle chatter. What you hear in one place, the suttas say, you don't carry to another to split people apart.
neighbors.difference: Rama guards his words to honor his family and his father's queen. In the Buddha's teaching, right speech is one step of the Eightfold Path, a training of the mind toward freedom from suffering.
neighbors.shared: kind silence about someone can be a gift.
neighbors.sources: Samyutta Nikaya 45.8 (paraphrase) · Digha Nikaya 1, Brahmajala Sutta (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: religion is sincere counsel
neighbors.text: Today an old enemy of Rama told his own king the truth: pleasant speakers are easy to find; people who say hard, good things are rare. Muslims keep a saying of the Prophet close to that: religion is sincere counsel, nasiha. And the Qur'an's short Surah 103 says the ones who aren't lost "exhort one another to truth."
neighbors.difference: Maricha warns Ravana to save his king and his city from ruin. In the hadith, sincere counsel is owed to God, His book, His messenger, leaders and ordinary people alike: honesty, offered with care.
neighbors.shared: the friend who tells you the hard truth is a gift.
neighbors.sources: Sahih Muslim, Book of Faith, hadith of Tamim al-Dari (paraphrase) · Qur'an 103:3 (Pickthall 1930)

neighbors.heading: flatterer or friend
neighbors.text: Today Maricha warned Ravana that people who say pleasant things are easy to find, and people who say hard, useful things are rare. Plutarch, a Greek writer, wrote a whole essay on telling a flatterer from a friend. The flatterer copies you and praises everything, he says; the friend speaks frankly, like a doctor whose medicine stings because it heals.
neighbors.difference: Maricha's warning rests on who Rama is: dharma in bodily form, a truth bigger than any king. Plutarch's test is human and practical: do a friend's words serve your good, or only your mood?
neighbors.shared: honest words, kindly meant, are a rare kind of love.
neighbors.sources: Plutarch, Moralia, How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a life given for others
neighbors.text: Today an old vulture fought Ravana to protect a woman who wasn't his own, knowing he'd lose. Sikhs remember Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru. Tradition says Kashmiri Pandits came to him asking for help to keep their faith, and he went to Delhi and gave his life for their freedom. Sikhs call him Hind di Chadar, the shelter of India.
neighbors.difference: Jatayu fights with beak and talons, an old king keeping faith with his friend's son. At Delhi, Guru Tegh Bahadur didn't fight; he chose death over giving up the freedom to worship, and Sikhs honor him as a martyr.
neighbors.shared: protecting someone who isn't yours is still your business.
neighbors.sources: Bachittar Natak, Dasam Granth (paraphrase) · Sikh tradition

neighbors.heading: greater love
neighbors.text: Today Jatayu, old and outmatched, told Ravana, not while I'm alive, and gave his wings to keep a promise. Christians hear Jesus at the last supper: "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends." They read it as a picture of the cross, and as a call to costly love.
neighbors.difference: Jatayu dies keeping faith with his friend Dasharatha. Christians believe Jesus laid down his life for everyone, friends and enemies alike, and rose again, and they see every other sacrifice in that light.
neighbors.shared: love keeps its promise even when it knows it'll lose.

neighbors.heading: practice that bears fruit
neighbors.text: Today Shabari, an old woman of the forest, said her years of practice bore fruit the day Rama came. Buddhists keep the verses of their own early women renunciants, the Therigatha. Again and again, these nuns, some old, some once poor or grieving, say in their own words that the long work is done and the mind is free.
neighbors.difference: For Shabari, the fruit is a visit: seeing Rama with her own eyes. In the Therigatha, the fruit isn't anyone's visit; it's freedom won through the nuns' own practice, with the Buddha's teaching pointing the way.
neighbors.shared: years of quiet practice are never wasted.

neighbors.heading: now let your servant go
neighbors.text: Today Shabari, who had waited years, said her practice bore fruit because she had seen Rama. Luke's Gospel has a man who had waited too. Simeon took the baby Jesus in his arms in the Temple and said, "Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace; because my eyes have seen thy salvation." The Church prays his words at night prayer.
neighbors.difference: Shabari welcomes Rama as an honored guest in her forest hermitage. For Catholics, Simeon holds God made flesh as a child, the long hope of his people arriving.
neighbors.shared: a lifetime of waiting can end in one bright meeting.
neighbors.sources: Luke 2:29–30 (Douay-Rheims) · Liturgy of the Hours, Night Prayer (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: let it ripen
neighbors.text: Today Rama waited out the monsoon in a cave, and Lakshmana told him to save his strength for the time to act. The Stoic teacher Epictetus put it plainly: nothing great comes about suddenly, not even a bunch of grapes or a fig. If you want a fig, he said, let it blossom first, then bear fruit, then ripen.
neighbors.difference: Rama's waiting holds grief and a vow: his wife is a captive and he must keep faith. Epictetus treats patience as reason at work, accepting what isn't in our power and tending what is.
neighbors.shared: waiting well is its own kind of strength.

neighbors.heading: a time to every purpose
neighbors.text: Today Rama couldn't search in the monsoon, so he waited in a cave and watched the rain. The Hebrew Bible makes room for seasons like that: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." Jewish prayer turns with the seasons too, adding words about wind and rain in the rainy months.
neighbors.difference: Rama waits because the roads are flooded and the rains decide. Ecclesiastes sees every season in God's hands, and its teacher admits people can't fully grasp why the times fall as they do.
neighbors.shared: some seasons ask us to wait, and that's allowed.
neighbors.sources: Ecclesiastes 3:1 (JPS 1917) · Ecclesiastes 3:11 (paraphrase) · the Amidah's rain blessing (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: seventy times seven
neighbors.text: Today Sugriva said, I may have slipped, who doesn't, and Rama took him back with an embrace. Christians remember Peter asking Jesus how often to forgive. Seven times? Jesus answered: "I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven." And in the Lord's Prayer, Christians ask to be forgiven as they forgive.
neighbors.difference: Sugriva's apology repairs a pact between friends and allies. For Christians, forgiving others is bound up with being forgiven by God, and many Christians teach it even when the other person never says sorry.
neighbors.shared: a friendship tested and repaired can come back stronger.

neighbors.heading: forgive and overlook
neighbors.text: Today Sugriva owned his slip, and Rama didn't hold the lost weeks against him. The Qur'an asks the same of believers: "Let them forgive and show indulgence. Yearn ye not that Allah may forgive you?" Commentators link the verse to Abu Bakr, who had sworn off helping a relative who wronged him, then forgave him and kept helping.
neighbors.difference: Rama's forgiveness is kshama, a king's patience, like the earth that bears everything. In the Qur'an, forgiving people is tied to hoping for God's forgiveness; one of God's names is Al-Ghafur, the Forgiving.
neighbors.shared: own the mistake, then let the friendship breathe again.

neighbors.heading: hoping for nothing
neighbors.text: Today Svayamprabha fed lost strangers, led them out of her cave, and asked for nothing back. Catholics hear Jesus in Luke's Gospel: "do good, and lend, hoping for nothing thereby: and your reward shall be great." The Church's works of mercy grow from words like these: feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, shelter the homeless.
neighbors.difference: Svayamprabha helps by the power of her own austerities, then disappears into the dark. For Catholics, mercy given freely is a way of meeting Christ in the person helped, made possible by God's grace.
neighbors.shared: the kindest help sometimes leaves without waiting for thanks.
neighbors.sources: Luke 6:35 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2447 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: seva, wanting nothing
neighbors.text: Today a woman in a cave gave food, rest and rescue to lost strangers, and wanted nothing back. Sikhs call that kind of help seva, selfless service. Sukhmani Sahib, a long hymn by Guru Arjan, says the one who serves without desire for reward reaches the Lord. You can see it in the gurdwara kitchen, where volunteers cook for anyone who walks in.
neighbors.difference: Svayamprabha is a solitary ascetic who helps by her own spiritual power. For Sikhs, seva is ordinary and shared, done by householders in kitchens and courtyards, as a way to wear down the ego.
neighbors.shared: help given freely is complete, even if no one remembers.
neighbors.sources: Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan, Guru Granth Sahib (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: mighty man of valor
neighbors.text: Today an old bear walked over to Hanuman and asked: why are you sitting there? The Bible has a scene like it. Gideon is hiding, threshing wheat in a winepress, when an angel greets him: "The LORD is with thee, thou mighty man of valour." Gideon protests that he's the least in his father's house. His strength is named out loud before he feels it.
neighbors.difference: Jambavan reminds Hanuman of strength he was born with, his father the wind's own speed. In Judges, Gideon's strength comes from God being with him, and the story insists the victory is God's.
neighbors.shared: sometimes strength comes back when someone says it out loud.

neighbors.heading: the mind was bright all along
neighbors.text: Today Hanuman sat apart, his strength forgotten, until someone told him his own story. Buddhists have a teaching that sounds close. In the Anguttara Nikaya, the Buddha says the mind is luminous, and it's stained by defilements that arrive from outside. Practice doesn't build the brightness from nothing; it clears away what covered it.
neighbors.difference: Hanuman's strength is a gift from his father, Vayu, and he gets it back by remembering who he is. The Buddha's luminous mind isn't a lasting self or a god's gift; it's clarity uncovered by training.
neighbors.shared: what you've forgotten about yourself may still be there.
neighbors.sources: Anguttara Nikaya, Book of Ones, the luminous mind passage (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: despair not
neighbors.text: Today Hanuman searched every room, found nothing, and fell into despair, then got up again: not giving in to despair is the root of good fortune. In the Qur'an, the prophet Jacob, still grieving his lost son Joseph, sends his sons out searching and tells them, "despair not of the Spirit of Allah."
neighbors.difference: Hanuman talks himself back up and bows to Rama, Sita and the gods before he searches again. For Jacob, hope rests on God's mercy alone, and the verse says only those without faith despair of it.
neighbors.shared: keep looking; giving up isn't the only door left.

neighbors.heading: belief helps create the fact
neighbors.text: Today Hanuman sank into despair in Ravana's palace, and climbed back out more than once. The psychologist and philosopher William James wrote about that climb. In a talk called "Is Life Worth Living?" he said: "Believe that life is worth living, and your belief will help create the fact." For James, hope is partly something you do.
neighbors.difference: Hanuman's hope leans on Rama and the gods; he bows to them before starting again. James grounds hope in what belief does inside a person: courage can open what doubt would have closed.
neighbors.shared: despair can sit with you without making the decision.
neighbors.sources: William James, "Is Life Worth Living?", in The Will to Believe

neighbors.heading: the Name, remembered
neighbors.text: Today Hanuman made sure the first thing Sita heard, frightened and alone, was the name she loved. Sikhs build a whole practice on that: naam simran, remembering the Name of God. Sukhmani Sahib opens by asking you to remember, and remember, and find peace. And the Gurus sang in the everyday languages people spoke, the way Hanuman chose plain words.
neighbors.difference: Hanuman speaks Rama's name to comfort Sita: her husband's name and, for many Hindus, God's. For Sikhs, the Name is God's presence beyond any one form, repeated so the mind stays near it.
neighbors.shared: a loved name, spoken softly, can steady a frightened heart.
neighbors.sources: Sukhmani Sahib, opening, Guru Granth Sahib (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: she heard her name
neighbors.text: Today Hanuman spoke softly from the branches so Sita would hear Rama's name before anything frightening. John's Gospel has a grieving woman in a garden too. Mary Magdalene, weeping at the empty tomb, doesn't know who's speaking, until he says one word: "Mary." She turns and answers, "Rabboni; which is to say, Master."
neighbors.difference: Sita hears her husband's name from a messenger, and learns he's searching for her. Mary hears her own name from Jesus himself, and Christians read it as a first meeting with the risen Christ.
neighbors.shared: being named with love can turn grief toward hope.

neighbors.heading: the snake's old skin
neighbors.text: Today Hanuman, horrified at what his anger nearly did, praised the one who throws off anger the way a snake sheds its old skin. The Buddha used the same picture. The opening verse of the Uraga Sutta, the snake discourse, praises one who checks rising anger the way medicine checks a snake's venom, and lets go of this shore and the far shore, like a snake's worn-out skin.
neighbors.difference: Hanuman condemns his anger because it nearly hurt the one he came to save. For the Buddha, hatred is one of three fires he named, a root of suffering to be uprooted by practice.
neighbors.shared: anger can be set down, the way a snake leaves its skin.

neighbors.heading: be angry, and sin not
neighbors.text: Today Hanuman burned Lanka and then stood on the shore, sick with fear that his fury had harmed Sita. Catholics hear Saint Paul: "Be angry, and sin not. Let not the sun go down upon your anger." The Church counts anger among the capital sins when it becomes a wish for revenge, and teaches that it can be set right.
neighbors.difference: Hanuman learns from his own scare, and relief comes from voices in the sky. For Catholics, sin is healed by God's grace, and in confession anger that did harm can be named and forgiven.
neighbors.shared: the moment after anger is where wisdom can begin.
neighbors.sources: Ephesians 4:26 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1866, 2302 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: unhistoric acts
neighbors.text: Today a whole army of monkeys and bears built a bridge in five days, and later tellers added a squirrel rolling in sand to help. The novelist George Eliot ended Middlemarch with a line that honors that squirrel's kind of work: "the growing good of the world is partly dependent on unhistoric acts." Small, unseen work holds up big things.
neighbors.difference: In the Ramayana tradition, the bridge is built for Rama, and the squirrel's small gift is told as a lesson in devotion. Eliot's line asks for no particular faith: the good done by quiet, ordinary lives is worth honoring in itself.
neighbors.shared: no gift is too small for the bridge.

neighbors.heading: a mind to work
neighbors.text: Today an army built a bridge across the sea, everyone carrying stones. The Hebrew Bible tells of a whole people rebuilding Jerusalem's wall, many repairing the stretch beside their own homes. Nehemiah sums it up: "So built we the wall... for the people had a mind to work." And the Mishnah adds: you needn't finish the work, but you aren't free to stop.
neighbors.difference: Rama's bridge is built in five days for a rescue, held up by an ocean's promise. Nehemiah's wall is rebuilt to restore a city after exile, and the work goes on under threat.
neighbors.shared: everyone carries a stone, and the bridge holds.
neighbors.sources: Nehemiah 3 (paraphrase) · Nehemiah 4:6 (KJV; 3:38 in Jewish Bibles) · Pirkei Avot 2:16 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: I will in no wise cast out
neighbors.text: Today Rama vowed safety to anyone who comes even once and says, I am yours, even if it were Ravana himself. Christians hear Jesus in John's Gospel: "him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out." And in the Sermon on the Mount he said, "Love your enemies," and pray for those who persecute you.
neighbors.difference: Rama makes his vow as a king and, for many devotees, as God giving refuge, sharanagati. Christians believe that welcome comes through Jesus, whose death and rising they trust opens the door to anyone who turns to him.
neighbors.shared: the door stays open, even for someone from the other side.

neighbors.heading: grant him protection
neighbors.text: Today the enemy king's brother asked for refuge, and Rama said yes, and would have even for Ravana. The Qur'an has a command like it. If one of the idolaters at war with the believers asks for protection, it says, grant it, so he may hear the word of God, then escort him to a place where he is safe.
neighbors.difference: Rama's vow takes in anyone who says, I am yours, and makes him a friend. The Qur'an's protection asks nothing like that: the one who asks hears God's word and is taken safely home.
neighbors.shared: someone asking for safety should find it.

neighbors.heading: the angel who heals
neighbors.text: Today Hanuman carried a mountain of healing herbs through the night, and became the one people pray to when someone they love is sick. Catholics have a healer sent from heaven too. In the Book of Tobit, the angel Raphael travels in disguise, shows young Tobias a remedy, and old Tobit's blindness is cured. Then Raphael reveals who he is.
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, Hanuman is himself divine and prayed to directly. For Catholics, Raphael is an angel, a creature serving God, honored and asked to pray, while healing comes from God alone.
neighbors.shared: help can arrive at night, just when everyone feels helpless.

neighbors.heading: a Guru's herb garden
neighbors.text: Today Hanuman carried healing herbs through the night and became the one people pray to when someone's in the hospital. Sikhs remember Guru Har Rai, the seventh Guru, who tradition says kept a herb garden and a dispensary. When the emperor's son fell ill and the court's doctors failed, the Guru sent the medicine he needed, though that family had been no friend.
neighbors.difference: Hanuman's flight is a wonder of strength and devotion, a mountain carried in a night. Guru Har Rai's healing is remembered as plain seva: herbs grown and medicine given, to friend or foe.
neighbors.shared: healing belongs to everyone, friend or not.
neighbors.sources: Sikh tradition about Guru Har Rai (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: when your enemy falls
neighbors.text: Today Rama said enmity ends at death, and gave Ravana a king's funeral. The Hebrew Bible says, "Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth." The Talmud tells that when Egypt's army drowned in the sea, the angels wanted to sing, and God stopped them: the work of my hands is drowning, and you would sing?
neighbors.difference: Rama honors Ravana as a great warrior and calls him his own now. The Talmud still celebrates the rescue: Israel sang at the sea. What it refuses is joy at the enemy's death itself.
neighbors.shared: when the fight is over, the hatred can end too.

neighbors.heading: hatred ceases by love
neighbors.text: Today Rama refused to carry hatred one step past Ravana's death, and Sita spared the guards who'd tormented her. The Dhammapada opens close to this. Whoever keeps thinking, he abused me, he beat me, never lets hatred end. Then: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule."
neighbors.difference: Rama honors Ravana with royal rites, a king's duty kept even for an enemy. The Buddha's teaching looks inward: letting go of hatred is part of freeing your own mind, whoever the enemy was.
neighbors.shared: hatred stops where someone finally refuses to pass it on.

neighbors.heading: return the trust
neighbors.text: Today Bharata put the sandals back on Rama's feet and said the kingdom was a deposit left with him; he was giving it back. Muslims call such a trust amanah. The Qur'an says, "Lo! Allah commandeth you that ye restore deposits to their owners," and the Prophet was known, even before his calling, as al-Amin, the trustworthy.
neighbors.difference: Bharata returns a throne to his brother, keeping faith with Rama and their father's word. In Islam, every trust, even your own life and gifts, is held from God, and keeping it is part of worship.
neighbors.shared: what's left in your care deserves to go back whole.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 4:58 (Pickthall 1930) · Ibn Ishaq, Life of the Messenger of God (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: good faith
neighbors.text: Today Bharata handed back a kingdom he'd held for fourteen years: a promise kept on both sides. The Roman philosopher Cicero wrote that the foundation of justice is good faith, truth and faithfulness to promises and agreements. He even asks when a deposit should be returned, and answers that justice usually means giving back what was trusted to you.
neighbors.difference: Bharata keeps faith out of love and dharma, his whole life shaped around the brother he waits for. Cicero roots good faith in reason and the bonds of society, a duty owed to friend and stranger alike.
neighbors.shared: a promise kept on both sides can feel like coming home.

items.lessonTitle: Janmashtami: the night Krishna was born

neighbors.heading: a child carried to safety
neighbors.text: Today a baby was born at midnight in a tyrant's prison and carried across a river to safety. Christians tell of a child hunted by a king too. After Jesus is born, Joseph is warned in a dream: "Arise, and take the young child and his mother, and flee into Egypt." He leaves by night. Some churches mark Christmas at midnight.
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, Krishna is God appearing in the world, first in divine form, then as a baby. Christians believe God became human once, in Jesus, fully God and fully human, born to save the world.
neighbors.shared: the good can arrive in the darkest, most locked-up place.

neighbors.heading: the mist cleared
neighbors.text: Today we kept Krishna's birthday, waiting up for the good to arrive in the dark. Sikhs keep birthdays too: Gurpurabs, the Gurus' birthdays, with hymns, prayers and processions. Of Guru Nanak's coming, Bhai Gurdas wrote that when the true Guru Nanak appeared, the mist cleared and light spread through the world.
neighbors.difference: Many Hindus celebrate Krishna's birth as God come down in a body. The Mool Mantar calls God ajooni, beyond birth, and Sikhs honor Guru Nanak as the Guru who brought God's light into the world.
neighbors.shared: a birthday can be a way of saying the light came.
neighbors.sources: Bhai Gurdas, Var 1, pauri 27 (paraphrase) · Mool Mantar, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 1 (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva

neighbors.heading: the awakened one
neighbors.text: Today we kept Shivaratri, the night you don't sleep through. Buddhists carry wakefulness in their teacher's very title: Buddha means the awakened one. The Dhammapada says, "Earnestness is the path of immortality (Nirvâna), thoughtlessness the path of death." On observance days, some Buddhists keep extra precepts, and some sit in meditation through the night.
neighbors.difference: On Shivaratri the vigil is devotion: water, bilva leaves and Shiva's name until dawn. For Buddhists, wakefulness is above all a state of mind, clear attention trained day by day, not a night kept for a god.
neighbors.shared: don't sleep through the moments that matter.

neighbors.heading: watch and pray
neighbors.text: Today many Hindus stayed awake for Shiva until dawn. Catholics keep a great night vigil too. On Holy Saturday the Easter Vigil begins in the dark, with a new fire and one candle carried into the church. And Jesus, in the garden before his arrest, asked his friends: "Watch ye, and pray that ye enter not into temptation."
neighbors.difference: Shivaratri honors Shiva with fasting, water and bilva leaves on the lingam. The Easter Vigil keeps watch for Christ's rising from the dead, which Catholics hold as the center of their faith.
neighbors.shared: some nights are worth staying awake for.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 26:41 (Douay-Rheims) · Roman Missal, the Easter Vigil (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: guests in a hut
neighbors.text: Today Ganesha left home for the water, and the crowd shouted, come back soon. Jews keep a festival of a temporary home. At Sukkot the Torah says, "Ye shall dwell in booths seven days." Families build a sukkah, eat in it, and by an old custom welcome honored guests, the ushpizin: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and others. Then it comes down until next year.
neighbors.difference: Ganesha is welcomed home as a divine guest, then released to the water. The sukkah remembers Israel's journey through the wilderness in God's care, and its guests are honored ancestors, welcomed in spirit.
neighbors.shared: you can love something fully and still let it go.
neighbors.sources: Leviticus 23:42 (JPS 1917) · Leviticus 23:43 (paraphrase) · the ushpizin custom, from the Zohar (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: I have given it back
neighbors.text: Today a crowd carried Ganesha into the water, crying, and called out: come back soon. The Stoic teacher Epictetus gave advice for moments like that. Never say of anything, I have lost it, he wrote; say, I have given it back. Enjoy what you have the way a traveler enjoys an inn: fully, knowing it isn't yours to keep.
neighbors.difference: Visarjan is worship: the family offers food, asks forgiveness, and hopes Ganesha will return. Epictetus's letting go is a discipline of reason, accepting that what we love was never ours to control.
neighbors.shared: letting go and looking forward can share one breath.

items.lessonTitle: karma — the Isha Upanishad as a life

neighbors.heading: the earth is the LORD's
neighbors.text: Today the Isha Upanishad asked, whose, after all, is wealth? Christians pray a psalm that answers: "The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein." Jesus told of a rich man who built bigger barns, then heard that his life would be required of him that night. Many Christians call the answer stewardship.
neighbors.difference: The Isha speaks of a world dwelt in by the Lord, and Shankara reads its line as letting go of owning. Christians see a Creator distinct from creation, who entrusts it to people to care for and share.
neighbors.shared: hold what you have like something borrowed, and enjoy it.

neighbors.heading: made trustees
neighbors.text: Today the Isha Upanishad asked, whose, after all, is wealth? The Qur'an answers that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God, and tells believers to "spend of that whereof He hath made you trustees." Zakat, a yearly giving, is one of Islam's five pillars, a reminder that wealth was never only yours.
neighbors.difference: The Isha opens a path where, for some readers, letting go of owning leads toward knowing the Self. In Islam, God alone is owner, beyond all creation, and people are trustees who will answer for how they spent.
neighbors.shared: what passes through your hands was lent, not given forever.

items.lessonTitle: bhakti — the Narada Bhakti Sutras opening

neighbors.heading: restless till it rests
neighbors.text: Today Narada said love for God shows in the ache of forgetting him. Catholics hear Saint Augustine, who opens his Confessions speaking straight to God: "Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee." For Augustine, the ache isn't a failure. It's the heart pointing home.
neighbors.difference: Narada points to the gopis' love for Krishna, and sets several teachers' marks of devotion side by side. Augustine's longing turns toward the God he came to know in Christ, and he tells it as his own life's story.
neighbors.shared: missing God can itself be a kind of love.

neighbors.heading: forgetting, I die
neighbors.text: Today the Narada Bhakti Sutras said real love feels anguish at forgetting the beloved. Guru Nanak sang it in a hymn Sikhs pray in the evening: aakhaa jeevaa, visrai mar jaao. Remembering, I live; forgetting, I die. That's why naam simran, remembering the Name, runs through a Sikh day, from early morning to night prayers.
neighbors.difference: Narada pictures devotion through the gopis' love for Krishna, God with a form and a story. Sikhs love the Formless One, Nirankar, remembered through the Name and the Guru's word.
neighbors.shared: love shows in how much it hurts to forget.
neighbors.sources: Guru Nanak, Raag Asa, in Rehras Sahib, Guru Granth Sahib (paraphrase)
